name: GAMBIT
expansion: Game-Theoretic Analysis of Model Behavior & Interactions

intro.problem: A two-network background estimate [@abcdisco2021] needs its input features split between the networks, and that split is usually made by hand even though features interact and the choice directly decides how well the estimate closes.
intro.value: A principled, data-driven partition would make the background estimate more defensible and show which features actually drive closure, extending distance-correlation feature selection [@das2024] from one network to the assignment between two.
intro.approach: GAMBIT mixes two kinds of game. In the cooperative game the features are players and each is credited by its marginal contribution against permutation nulls [@shapley1953][@cohen2005]; in the adversarial game the two networks are players competing for features [@monderer1996][@rosenthal1973]. The cooperative stage prunes the pool, the adversarial stage places what remains, and every result is re-measured on seeds disjoint from the selection.
intro.goals: The next phase re-reads two weeks of games, all refereed by a dependence statistic, against the closure metric the analysis actually reports, then re-runs the games with closure as the referee and states plainly what improved closure costs in discrimination.

questions: Which features actually drive background closure, rather than discrimination?
Does a partition found by mixing cooperative and adversarial play beat the hand-built one on held-out seeds?
Does the choice of referee change the answer: do games scored on closure pick different partitions from games scored on dependence?

timeline.label: Idea set: the two networks compete for input features, with background-estimate closure as the shared stake
Program fixed: plain baseline first, then one adversarial game and one cooperative game
Cooperative scoring rebuilt so selection and evaluation no longer share the same noise
First end-to-end run on the barrel: cooperative selection fed into the adversarial game
Knockout, pruning and registry games run in both regions
Review deck covering all builds; project officially named GAMBIT
Re-read every recorded game against the closure metric, offline, with no retraining
Measure how often the dependence referee and the closure metric agree on a move
Re-run the games on new data with closure as the referee
Wire the data gates and block reduction ahead of selection; run the endcap end to end

tagline: Cooperative and adversarial feature games for the ABCD networks

components.name: Cooperative game
components.subtitle: Features as players
components.summary: Each feature's worth is its average marginal contribution to the background estimate [@shapley1953], measured against permutation nulls that give every network its own zero point, so selection needs no hand-chosen threshold [@cohen2005]. Exact values on small subsets, sampled values on the full registry [@wang2022].

items.label: Leave-one-out
items.detail: Every feature scored against shuffled copies of real columns, per network

items.label: Knockout
items.detail: Remove features jointly and check both discrimination and closure

items.label: Pruning
items.detail: Correlated feature families reduced to representatives before selection

components.name: Adversarial game
components.subtitle: Networks as players
components.summary: The two networks take turns claiming, releasing or dropping features, and a move stands only if it beats a measured noise floor. Equilibrium is not guaranteed: coalitions can remove pure equilibria [@kuniavsky2011], and slow convergence can look like none [@panageas2023].

items.label: Moves
items.detail: Claim from the other network, claim from the free pool, or drop

items.label: Gate
items.detail: Paired seeds, a measured floor and a null harness decide whether a move counts

items.label: Worst case
items.detail: Weakest signal mass point kept in the payoff, not the loss [@sagawa2019]

components.name: Pipeline
components.subtitle: Cooperative into adversarial
components.summary: The cooperative stage hands a pruned pool to the adversarial stage, and the result is promoted and graded on seeds neither search ever used. Built and run end to end on the barrel; the endcap run and the upstream data gates are next.

results.title: First selection-free comparison
results.text: On the barrel, the partition found by the pipeline closed substantially better than the hand-built one on held-out seeds, but the second network lost discrimination. It is a trade with a confound, not a win.

results.title: Discrimination is not closure
results.text: Barrel features that add nothing to discrimination still do work for factorization; removing them degrades the background estimate. A feature is only safe to drop when both axes clear.

results.title: Most endcap features are jointly removable
results.text: In the endcap, a large share of the first network's inputs can be removed together with no cost on either axis, until a deeper knockout trades discrimination away for closure.

results.title: Equilibrium in one region, cycling in the other
results.text: The endcap game settles quickly; the barrel game cycles. Two features that both networks want and neither can keep explain the cycling, and a disjoint partition cannot express a fix.

results.title: The referee was the wrong statistic
results.text: Every recorded game was scored on a dependence test that tracks reported closure poorly, so all of the above is first-generation until it is re-read against closure.
